slides.title: What is a Binary Search Tree?

blocks.text: A binary search tree is a binary tree with the added property that for each node:
The left child contains an element which is less than the element stored in the parent node.
The right child contains an element which is greater than or equal to the element stored in the parent node.
Adding an element to a binary search tree or removing an element should be done without violating its main property.

slides.title: Searching a Binary Search Tree

blocks.text: To determine if a particular target element exists in a tree:
Start at the root node
Compare the target with the element at the current node
Move left if the target is less than the element at the current node
Move right if target is greater than the element at the current node
Stop at the current node if the target element is found
We either find the target element or encounter the end of a path and conclude that the target is not found.

slides.title: Removing a Node in a Binary Search Tree

blocks.text: Removing a target node in a Binary Search Tree (BST) is not as simple as that for a linear data structure.
After removing a node, the resulting tree must still be valid.
Three distinct situations must be considered when removing a node in a binary search tree.
The node to remove is a leaf
The node to remove has one child
The node to remove has two children

slides.title: Summary of Removing a Node

blocks.text: Case 1: Node is a leaf and can be simply deleted
Case 2: Node has only one child
It is removed by relinking its parent node to its only child node
Case 3: Node has two children
The in-order successor is the smallest element in the right subtree
The element to be removed is replaced with its in-order successor
The in-order successor node does NOT have a left child
The in-order successor node is removed as in case 1 or 2

slides.title: Operations on a Binary Search Tree

blocks.text: The definition of a binary search tree is an extension to the definition of a binary tree. The following operations are defined in addition to the ones defined on a binary tree.

slides.title: Properties of Binary Search Trees

blocks.text: The shape of a binary search tree depends on the order in which the elements are added and removed.
In a balanced binary search tree, the maximum number of nodes at level l is 2l.
In a balanced binary search tree of height h, all the levels are fully populated, except for the last level. The number of nodes is N = O(2h). If the tree is full then N = 2h+1 – 1.
In a balanced binary search tree with N nodes, the height of the tree is h = O(log2 N).

slides.title: Benefits of Binary Search Trees

blocks.text: Efficient searching
Searching for an element is O(log2 N) for a balanced BST, where log2 N is approximately the height of a balanced BST with N nodes.
Finding the minimum and maximum element is also O((log2 N) for a balanced BST.
Efficient insertion and deletion of elements
Adding and removing an element is O(log2 N) for a balanced BST.
Ordered Structure
The get a sorted list of elements, perform in-order traversal of BST, which is O(N), because all N nodes are traversed.

slides.title: Applications of Binary Search Trees

blocks.text: Databases: BSTs are often used to implement database indexes, which allow for fast searching and retrieval of data.
File systems: BSTs are often used to store and organize files. For example, Unix uses a BST to store file names.
Network routing: Each node in the BST represents a destination for fast lookup and routing of packets through the network.
Dictionary implementations: Many programming languages provide built-in support for dictionaries, which are implemented using BSTs.
Game development: Binary search trees can be used in game development to store and search for game objects.

slides.title: Balancing Binary Search Trees

blocks.text: Our implementation does not ensure the BST stays balanced
Other approaches do, such as AVL and Red/Black trees
We will explore rotations – operations on binary search trees to assist in the process of keeping a tree balanced
Rotations show the basic algorithmic steps that are used to balance binary search trees
Our goal is to keep the maximum path length and the height of the tree to become h = log2 N

slides.title: Right Rotation

blocks.text: A rotation can be performed around the root of a tree. It corrects the imbalance caused by a long path in the subtree
A right rotation makes the left child the new root, the former root the new right child, and the right child of the former left child the new left child of the former root.

slides.title: AVL Trees

blocks.text: An AVL tree, named after its inventors (Adelson, Velskii, and Landis) ensures a Binary Search Tree remains balanced
For each node in the tree there is a numeric balance factor, which is the difference between the heights of its subtrees
After each add or removal of a node, the balance factors are checked and rotations performed as needed
If the balance factor of a node is -2, it means that the node's right subtree has a height shorter than the left subtree by 2

slides.title: Right Rotation in an AVL Tree

blocks.text: A tree or a subtree can be unbalanced after the insertion or removal of a node. The balance factors are updated at the point of insertion and up towards the root. If the tree becomes unbalanced, rotation is applied.

slides.title: RightLeft Rotation in an AVL Tree

blocks.text: After removing node 3, the balance factor in the root node becomes +2
The balance factor of the right child is –1. This means that the left subtree of the right child is longer
To balance the tree, a right rotation is performed around the right child
Then a left rotation is performed around the root.
The balance factors are updated, and tree becomes balanced.
